title: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
description: Binary search on value range rather than index, counting elements less than or equal to a candidate.

data.text: Given an `n x n` matrix where each row and column is sorted in ascending order, find the `k`th smallest element (1-indexed). Note it is the `k`th smallest, not necessarily distinct.

The answer lies between `matrix[0][0]` and `matrix[n-1][n-1]`. For a candidate value `mid`, count how many elements are `<= mid` by walking each row's sorted order with a pointer (or binary search per row) — `O(n log n)` or `O(n)` with two pointers. If the count `>= k`, the answer is `mid` or smaller (move right bound down); else move the left bound up. This is `O(log(range) * n)` time, `O(1)` space — it searches the *value* space, not the index space.

data.title: Binary search on value O(n log R)

data.text: Maintain a max-heap holding the `k` smallest elements seen. Iterate every cell; push it and, if the heap exceeds `k` elements, pop the largest. At the end the heap top is the `k`th smallest. This is `O(n^2 log k)` time and `O(k)` space, and works for matrices with looser ordering.

data.title: Bounded max-heap O(n^2 log k)

data.caption: Binary search on the value range: count elements <= mid, then narrow to the half that must contain the kth smallest.

data.title: What improved?
data.text: Sorting all n^2 elements is O(n^2 log(n^2)). Binary search on value asks 'how many elements are <= mid', turning the search space into the value range. The heap approach is simpler to reason about but slower unless k is small relative to n^2.
